title: What Is the Maximum Length of a Dryer Vent?
h1: What Is the Maximum Distance You Can Run a Dryer Vent?
description: California code limits a 4-inch dryer vent to 14 feet with two elbows unless the dryer maker allows more. Learn how to measure yours and fix a long run.
quick_answer: In California, the default rule allows a 4-inch dryer vent to run 14 feet in total, including two 90-degree elbows, and you subtract 2 feet for each extra elbow. Your dryer's installation manual can allow a longer run, and many do, as long as the local building department accepts it. The 35-foot figure often quoted online comes from a different code.
body:
Long dryer vents are one of the most common problems we see. Lint builds up faster, clothes take longer to dry and the dryer runs hotter than it should. Knowing the maximum length helps you spot a vent that's working against you.

How is dryer vent length measured in California?

The California Mechanical Code sets a default limit of 14 feet of duct, counting both horizontal and vertical runs, with up to two 90-degree elbows included. Every 90-degree elbow beyond those two takes 2 feet off the allowed length.

  1. Measure the duct from the dryer connection to where the vent leaves the house, including any vertical rise to the roof.
  2. Count the 90-degree elbows.
  3. Subtract 2 feet from the 14-foot limit for each elbow past the second.
  4. Compare your measured length to that limit.

For example, a run with four 90-degree elbows is limited to 10 feet under the default rule. Plenty of laundry rooms in the middle of a house need more than that, which is where the dryer manufacturer's chart comes in.

The flexible transition duct behind the dryer should be a listed metal connector, never plastic or thin foil, and California's code limits it to 6 feet. Shorter is better.

What if the manufacturer allows a longer run?

The code lets you follow the dryer manufacturer's installation instructions when they allow a different length, as long as the local building department accepts it. Most dryer manuals include a venting chart that lists the maximum run for different numbers of elbows and hood styles, and many allow more than 14 feet. If you replace the dryer later, check the new model's chart, since limits vary between models.

You may also see 35 feet quoted online. That number comes from a different model code, not the California Mechanical Code, so don't rely on it for a local install.

Why does a long dryer vent cause problems?

  • Slow drying. Moist air can't escape fast enough, so loads take two cycles.
  • Lint buildup. Slower airflow lets lint settle, especially in elbows and low spots.
  • Fire risk. Lint is highly flammable, and a dryer that runs hot with poor airflow is a real hazard.
  • Wear on the dryer. Heating elements, thermostats and motors work harder and fail sooner.
  • Moisture problems. A long, sagging vent through an attic can collect condensation.

Where do long dryer vents show up in Southern California homes?

In many local homes, the laundry sits in an interior room, a hallway closet or the garage. The vent then has to travel up through the attic and out the roof, or across the attic to a side wall. Condos and two-story homes often have long, hidden runs with several turns. Laundry rooms added during remodels sometimes ended up with vents that were never designed for the distance.

What can you do if your vent is too long?

  • Reroute the vent. A shorter, straighter path to the outside is the best fix when it's possible.
  • Replace elbows. Swapping sharp 90-degree turns for two 45s, or using long-radius elbows, can reduce resistance.
  • Use smooth rigid metal duct. Ribbed flex duct traps lint and adds resistance.
  • Add a dryer booster fan. A listed booster fan can help on runs that can't be shortened, when installed per its instructions.
  • Clean the vent more often. Long runs collect lint faster and need regular cleaning.

Never use screws that poke into the duct, since they catch lint. Joints should be secured with foil tape or clamps.

Does vent size affect the maximum length?

Yes. The length limits assume a 4-inch diameter duct, which is the standard for residential dryers. Using a smaller duct reduces airflow and isn't allowed. Going larger isn't a fix either, since bigger duct slows the air down and lets lint settle. Stick with 4-inch smooth metal duct unless the dryer manufacturer specifies something else. Commercial and stacked laundry setups can have different requirements.

How do you know if your vent needs attention?

Watch for loads that take longer than usual, a dryer that's hot to the touch, a burning smell or weak airflow at the outside hood. If you notice any of these, have the vent checked. Our dryer vent team cleans, repairs and reroutes vents and can tell you whether your run is within limits.
faqs: Does the flexible hose behind the dryer count toward the maximum length?

Check your dryer's venting chart, since manufacturers handle it differently. Either way, it should be a listed metal transition duct no longer than 6 feet. It should never be plastic or thin foil, and it shouldn't be crushed behind the dryer.
Can a dryer vent go through the roof?

Yes, roof vents are common in Southern California homes with interior laundry rooms. They need a proper roof cap that doesn't have a screen, and they tend to collect lint faster, so plan on regular cleaning.
A booster fan that's listed for dryer use and installed according to its instructions can help a long vent. It's not a fix for a clogged or crushed vent, so clean and repair the duct first.
Is it OK to use a screen on the outside dryer vent?
No. Screens catch lint and block airflow. The outside hood should have a damper flap that opens when the dryer runs and closes to keep pests out.
